01 / Problem & Objectives

Problem & Design Objectives

Drivers may not notice how quickly a vehicle behind them is approaching. Our team built a prototype to warn them when an object gets too close or approaches too fast.

We initially focused on left-lane driving behavior, but shifted to a more general rear-approach warning system. We wanted it to give reliable readings and warnings, be affordable and easy to install, and stay out of the way during normal driving.

02 / System Design

System Design

The system uses two Arduino microcontrollers in separate 3D-printed enclosures. A LiDARLite v3 distance sensor sits at the back of the car. The rear Arduino sends its readings to the interior Arduino through long-range nRF24L01 radio modules.

The receiver calculates closing speed from changes in distance over time and uses a rolling average to reduce fluctuations in the estimate. An approximately 2-inch OLED shows distance and closing speed. When an object gets too close or approaches too fast, the screen displays a warning and an MP3 module plays an alert through a speaker.

Early versions used an ultrasonic sensor. We switched to LiDAR for longer-range measurements and upgraded the radios, display, and speaker as we worked through the design.

  1. LiDAR sensor
  2. Transmitting Arduino
  3. nRF24L01 wireless link
  4. Receiving Arduino
  5. OLED & speaker
03 / My Contributions

Individual Contributions

I handled nearly all of the software development and iteration, including deciding how the system should behave. I set up wireless data transfer, processed the LiDAR readings, and implemented the closing-speed calculation and rolling average.

I developed the warning logic and integrated the OLED display and audio module, including the timing of audible alerts.

For the enclosures, I adjusted the tolerances on an existing design before printing. The electronics and enclosure work were shared across the team.

04 / Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting & Iteration

Isolating a Wireless Failure

When the radios stopped communicating reliably, I initially thought the problem was in the code. I stripped the software back to basic transmitter and receiver test programs and swapped radio modules between Arduino boards. By checking one part at a time, I traced the problem to a faulty ground connection.

Stabilizing Readings & Warnings

Early versions gave inconsistent speed estimates, invalid distances, and warnings that shouldn’t have triggered. I adjusted how the code processed distance readings, averaged speed, and triggered warnings, then tested it again. I also changed the audio timing to address delayed or inappropriate alerts.

Fitting the Final Electronics

We tried several displays before settling on the larger OLED. The team revised the enclosures to fit it and the larger speaker.

05 / Testing & Results

Testing & Results

We mounted the prototype on my Mini Cooper Clubman and confirmed that the rear sensor could send readings to the receiver inside the car. We tested it with people walking and running toward the sensor, demonstrated the fast-approach and too-close warnings, and saw distance readings reach about 128 feet.

We haven’t tested it with moving vehicles yet, so we still need to check how accurately and reliably it works in those conditions.

The total hardware cost was about $242, including a $150 LiDAR sensor that we borrowed from the ITLL. That brought the remaining component cost to $92.

06 / Lessons & Next Steps

Reflection & Future Work

I had programming and CAD experience going in, but this project taught me more about working with physical electronics. Troubleshooting worked best when I separated the hardware and software and tested one part at a time.

Next time, I would order parts sooner and test them before spending as much time on the enclosures. We refined the housings before confirming that the components inside would work, so later hardware changes created extra work.

Other possible improvements include using a camera to identify vehicles, making the enclosures smaller, and improving the mounts.

07 / Expo & Recognition

Expo & Recognition

We brought the working prototype to CU Boulder’s Engineering Projects Expo on November 14, 2026, where we received the APEX Innovation Award from the CU Racing Team.

Big Kahunas was our five-person team in Professor Dan Godrick’s GEEN 1400 class. I worked with Atahan Tosun, Carter Jenson, Jason Schwartz, and Ved Kadam.
